title: Immunotherapies: Checkpoint Inhibitors, CAR T Cells, Eculizumab and Rituximab
summary: Learn which brake each checkpoint inhibitor blocks, how CAR T cells are made and what they treat, what anti-C5 eculizumab and anti-CD20 rituximab do, and the lab check that goes with each: thyroid tests, cytokine release and B-cell aplasia, meningococcal risk with C3-mediated hemolysis, and hepatitis B screening.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 44 Hits 9 (checkpoint inhibitors), 10 (CAR T) and 12 (eculizumab, rituximab), checked against Vaddepally 2020, Yin 2023, Li 2025, Alnefaie 2022, Risitano 2019, McNamara 2017 (MMWR) and Salles 2017. Qualifications: the reviewer’s anti-CTLA-4 list omits tremelimumab (US approval October 2022); CAR T is approved for more than adult lymphoma and childhood leukaemia (CD19 products for mantle cell lymphoma and adult B-ALL; the paediatric indication covers children and young adults; BCMA-directed idecabtagene vicleucel for myeloma); eculizumab leaves C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis and a high meningococcal risk even after vaccination. Approval facts are US (FDA); Philippine registration status is not covered. Memory hooks are the lesson’s own. Not taught: rituximab in autoantibody disease beyond its licensed RA/GPA/MPA indications, CD21/EBV, dosing, ravulizumab and proximal inhibitors.

objectives: Match each checkpoint inhibitor to PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 and explain why blocking these brakes boosts anti-tumour T cells.
Describe how autologous CAR T cells are made and name their main targets and indications.
State the targets of eculizumab and rituximab and the safety-related laboratory checks for each of the four therapies.

scenes.title: Three new prescriptions, three lab checks
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three oncology and haematology orders arrive on one morning — (1) a melanoma patient starting pembrolizumab, with thyroid tests on the follow-up order set; (2) a lymphoma patient starting rituximab, with hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody ordered first; (3) a patient with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria starting eculizumab, whose chart asks for proof of meningococcal vaccination. Question token: “Why a different lab check for each drug?”

cues.text: Three new prescriptions arrive. A melanoma patient starts pembrolizumab, and thyroid tests are on the follow-up orders.
A lymphoma patient starts rituximab, and hepatitis B tests are ordered first. A patient with PNH starts eculizumab, and the chart asks for meningococcal vaccination.
Why does each drug come with a different lab check? Because each one steers a different part of the immune system.

props.label: Why a different lab check for each drug?

scenes.title: Brakes, kill switches and targets
scenes.altText: Schematic: four cards. (1) CD28 is a co-stimulatory “accelerator” on T cells; CTLA-4 is a co-inhibitory brake that binds CD80/CD86 with higher affinity than CD28 and outcompetes it. (2) PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells (also B cells, NK cells, MDSCs); its ligand PD-L1 is expressed on many tumour cells and haematopoietic cells, so tumours can switch T cells off. (3) Complement: cleavage of C5 into C5a and C5b leads to the C5b–C9 membrane attack complex (MAC). (4) CD20 and CD19 are B-cell-restricted surface antigens.

cues.text: T cells need an accelerator, CD28, and they also have brakes. CTLA-4 is a brake that grabs CD80 and CD86 more tightly than CD28 does, so the accelerator loses its partner.
PD-1 is a second brake on T cells. Its partner, PD-L1, sits on many tumour cells, so a tumour can switch an attacking T cell off.
Complement ends with a kill switch: C5 is split into C5a and C5b, and C5b starts the membrane attack complex, C5b to C9, that punches holes in cells.
Finally, B cells carry their own surface markers, CD19 and CD20. Each of these is a target for one of today’s therapies.

scenes.title: Four ways to steer the immune system
scenes.altText: Four drug cards. Checkpoint inhibitors (monoclonal antibodies): anti-PD-1 nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab; anti-PD-L1 atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab; anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab (first approved, 2011) and tremelimumab (US approval October 2022, with durvalumab, for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma). CAR T cells: leukapheresis of the patient’s own (autologous) T cells → gene transfer, often by a viral vector, of a chimeric antigen receptor (single-chain variable fragment + CD3ζ ± a 4-1BB or CD28 co-stimulatory domain) → expansion → lymphodepleting chemotherapy (often fludarabine/cyclophosphamide) → reinfusion 48–96 h later; about 3 weeks; antigen recognition is MHC-independent. US-approved products: CD19-directed (tisagenlecleucel: B-ALL in children and young adults and large B-cell lymphoma; axicabtagene ciloleucel and lisocabtagene maraleucel: large B-cell lymphoma; brexucabtagene autoleucel: mantle cell lymphoma, adult B-ALL) and BCMA-directed idecabtagene vicleucel (multiple myeloma, 2021). Eculizumab: humanised anti-C5 antibody that prevents C5 cleavage, so no MAC; US-licensed for PNH and atypical HUS. Rituximab: chimeric IgG1 anti-CD20 that kills B cells by complement-dependent cytotoxicity, ADCC, phagocytosis and direct apoptosis.

cues.text: Checkpoint inhibitors are antibodies that block the brakes. Nivolumab, pembrolizumab and cemiplimab block PD-1. Atezolizumab, avelumab and durvalumab block its ligand, PD-L1. Ipilimumab, and since 2022 in the United States tremelimumab, block CTLA-4.

CAR T cells are a living drug. The patient’s own T cells are collected, given a synthetic receptor that recognises a target such as CD19 without needing MHC, grown in the lab, and reinfused after lymphodepleting chemotherapy. The whole process takes about three weeks.
CD19 CAR T products treat B-cell leukaemia in children and young adults and several adult B-cell lymphomas, and a BCMA-directed product treats multiple myeloma.

Eculizumab binds C5 and stops it being split, so no membrane attack complex forms. It is licensed for PNH and atypical HUS. Rituximab binds CD20 and destroys B cells through complement, natural killer cells, phagocytes and apoptosis.

scenes.title: What the lab watches
scenes.altText: Monitoring table. Checkpoint inhibitors: immune-related adverse events (irAEs) — skin most common, then gastrointestinal, then endocrine (thyroid dysfunction, usually hypothyroidism after thyroiditis; hypophysitis; type 1 diabetes-like); primary hypothyroidism in about 6–9% on anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and about 16% on combined anti-PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-CTLA-4; TSH and T4 guide management. CAR T: cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity; CD19 CAR T cells also remove normal B cells (B-cell aplasia), managed with intravenous immunoglobulin. Eculizumab: 1,000- to 2,000-fold higher incidence of meningococcal disease; MenACWY and MenB vaccines recommended before treatment, yet 14 of 16 US cases (2008–2016) had at least one vaccine dose; PNH red cells still lack CD55, so C3 fragments coat them (detectable by flow cytometry) and liver/spleen macrophages remove them — C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis in 25–50% of treated patients. Rituximab: screen hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis B core antibody before treatment because of reactivation risk. Hook answers listed.

cues.text: Releasing T-cell brakes can also release attacks on the body. After skin and bowel, endocrine organs are hit most often, especially the thyroid. Primary hypothyroidism, often after thyroiditis, affects about six to nine percent of patients on PD-1 or PD-L1 blockers, more with combinations, so TSH and T4 guide care.
CAR T cells can trigger cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity, and CD19 CAR T cells also remove normal B cells. That B-cell aplasia is managed with intravenous immunoglobulin.

Eculizumab raises the rate of meningococcal disease a thousand to two thousand times. Vaccines against groups A, C, W, Y and B are recommended first, yet most US cases occurred in vaccinated patients. And because PNH red cells still lack CD55, C3 fragments coat them, and macrophages remove them outside the vessels.
Before rituximab, screen for hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody, because B-cell depletion can reactivate hepatitis B. Those are the three answers to the hook.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Atezolizumab is a PD-1 blocker” (✓ atezolizumab, avelumab and durvalumab bind the ligand PD-L1; nivolumab, pembrolizumab and cemiplimab bind PD-1); “A vaccinated patient on eculizumab is protected from meningococcus” (✓ risk stays high — 14 of 16 US cases had been vaccinated; act fast on symptoms); “Eculizumab stops all hemolysis in PNH” (✓ it blocks only the terminal step; C3 fragments still coat PNH red cells, causing extravascular hemolysis).

cues.text: Trap one: atezolizumab is a PD-1 blocker. No: atezolizumab, avelumab and durvalumab bind the ligand, PD-L1.
Trap two: a vaccinated patient on eculizumab is protected from meningococcus. No: most US cases had been vaccinated, so symptoms need urgent care.
Trap three: eculizumab stops all hemolysis in PNH. No: it blocks only the terminal step, and C3-coated red cells are still removed by macrophages.

scenes.title: Release, Rebuild, Remove, Restrain
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Four Rs” — RELEASE the brakes (checkpoint inhibitors: PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4); REBUILD the soldier (CAR T: the patient’s own T cell with a new receptor); REMOVE the B cells (rituximab, anti-CD20); RESTRAIN the final strike (eculizumab, anti-C5). Four tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid, the four Rs. Release the brakes: checkpoint inhibitors. Rebuild the soldier: CAR T cells. Remove the B cells: rituximab. Restrain the final strike: eculizumab.

Where it breaks: released brakes also free attacks on the thyroid and other organs; a rebuilt soldier is a living drug that can trigger cytokine release syndrome; and restraining only the final strike leaves earlier C3 coating, and the risk of meningococcus, in place.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: A living drug → cytokine release syndrome
Anti-C5 leaves C3 coating and meningococcal risk

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “ICI = PD-1 · PD-L1 · CTLA-4 brakes off → watch thyroid · CAR T = own T cells + new receptor → CRS, B-cell aplasia”, “Rituximab = anti-CD20 → hepatitis B screen first · eculizumab = anti-C5 → meningococcal risk, C3 hemolysis”.

cues.text: Checkpoint inhibitors release the PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 brakes, CAR T cells are a patient’s own T cells given a new receptor, rituximab removes CD20-positive B cells and eculizumab blocks C5, and each one brings its own lab check.

props.label: ICI: brakes off → thyroid · CAR T: own T cells → CRS, B-cell aplasia
Anti-CD20 → hepatitis B screen · anti-C5 → meningococcus, C3 hemolysis

explanation.what: Plain language: some cancer drugs take the brakes off T cells; CAR T therapy rebuilds a patient’s own T cells to hunt a target; rituximab wipes out B cells; eculizumab stops the last step of complement. Each changes immunity in a way the lab must watch. Scientific terms: immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, CD28, CD80/CD86, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), single-chain variable fragment (scFv), CD3ζ, leukapheresis, lymphodepletion, cytokine release syndrome (CRS), B-cell aplasia, C5, membrane attack complex (MAC), CD55/CD59, extravascular hemolysis, CD20, complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), immune-related adverse event (irAE).
explanation.why: CTLA-4 outcompetes CD28 for CD80/CD86 and PD-1/PD-L1 signalling dampens T cells, so blocking either restores anti-tumour T-cell activity but also lowers self-tolerance (irAEs). A CAR recognises antigen without MHC, and CD19 CAR T cells kill normal B cells too. Anti-C5 prevents MAC formation, but PNH cells lacking CD55 still collect C3 fragments, and loss of terminal complement leaves patients vulnerable to Neisseria meningitidis. B-cell depletion by rituximab can reactivate hepatitis B.
explanation.measure: Checkpoint inhibitors: thyroid tests (TSH, T4) for thyroid irAEs; hypothyroidism in about 6–9% on anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and about 16% on combinations. CAR T: monitor for CRS and neurotoxicity; B-cell aplasia treated with IVIG. Eculizumab: MenACWY and MenB vaccination before treatment, with ongoing vigilance; C3 fragments on PNH red cells detectable by flow cytometry. Rituximab: HBsAg and anti-HBc before treatment.
explanation.differs: Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab) vs anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab) vs anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab, tremelimumab); CAR T (cell therapy, MHC-independent) vs monoclonal antibodies; intravascular (MAC) vs C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis in PNH; anti-C5 (complement) vs anti-CD20 (B cells).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match a drug to its target, name the cell source and target of CAR T cells, explain persistent anaemia on eculizumab, recognise meningococcal risk, or pick hepatitis B screening before rituximab.

mnemonic.text: Four Rs: RELEASE the brakes (checkpoint inhibitors), REBUILD the soldier (CAR T), REMOVE the B cells (rituximab), RESTRAIN the final strike (eculizumab).
mnemonic.explanation: One verb per therapy, matched to what it does to immunity.
mnemonic.limitation: Releasing brakes also causes immune-related adverse events; CAR T is a living drug that can cause cytokine release syndrome; anti-C5 leaves C3 coating (extravascular hemolysis) and meningococcal risk.

analogyLimitations: Brake and kill-switch pictures are schematic; signalling is simplified.
Approval facts are US (FDA) as reported in the cited reviews and change over time.
takeaway: Checkpoint inhibitors release the PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 brakes, CAR T cells are a patient’s own T cells given a new receptor, rituximab removes CD20-positive B cells and eculizumab blocks C5, and each one brings its own lab check.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer is started on atezolizumab. Which molecule does this checkpoint inhibitor bind?

options.rationale: Correct. Atezolizumab, avelumab and durvalumab are anti-PD-L1 antibodies.
Incorrect. Nivolumab, pembrolizumab and cemiplimab bind the receptor PD-1.
Incorrect. Ipilimumab and tremelimumab block CTLA-4.
Incorrect. CD20 is the B-cell target of rituximab, not a T-cell checkpoint.

questions.stem: A patient with PNH has been on eculizumab for a year. Haemoglobin is still low with a high reticulocyte count, and flow cytometry shows C3 fragments on the PNH red cells. What best explains this?

options.text: C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis, because anti-C5 does not block early complement activation on cells lacking CD55
options.rationale: Correct. C5 blockade prevents the MAC, but C3 fragments still coat PNH red cells, which liver and spleen macrophages remove.

options.text: Eculizumab directly activates the membrane attack complex
options.rationale: Incorrect. Eculizumab prevents C5 cleavage and so prevents MAC formation.

options.text: The PNH clone has disappeared, so the red cells are now normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. C3 fragments are found on surviving PNH red cells, showing the clone persists.
Incorrect. Eculizumab targets C5, not CD20, and B-cell loss does not explain red-cell C3 coating.

questions.stem: A patient with B-cell lymphoma is about to start rituximab. Which laboratory screen is recommended before the first dose?

options.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis B core antibody
options.rationale: Correct. Screening for hepatitis B is recommended because rituximab can cause reactivation.
Incorrect. That is the safety step for the anti-C5 antibody eculizumab.

options.text: TSH and T4 for immune-related thyroiditis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Thyroid irAEs are associated with checkpoint inhibitors, not this anti-CD20 antibody.

options.text: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 on red cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Missing CD55 and CD59 on red cells is a feature of PNH, not a safety check before rituximab.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 44 Hit 9 lists ipilimumab as the anti-CTLA-4 agent; Li 2025 reports US approval of tremelimumab (anti-CTLA-4, with durvalumab, unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma) in October 2022. Drug lists are date-dependent (register flag rv-ctla4-tremelimumab).

Ch. 44 Hit 10 limits CAR T use to adult lymphoma and childhood leukaemia; Alnefaie 2022 lists the paediatric B-ALL indication as children and young adults, plus CD19 products for mantle cell lymphoma and adult B-ALL and BCMA-directed idecabtagene vicleucel for multiple myeloma (register flag rv-cart-indications-myeloma).

Ch. 44 Hit 12 says eculizumab treats PNH without noting that C3-mediated extravascular hemolysis persists in 25–50% of patients (Risitano 2019) and that meningococcal risk stays high despite vaccination (McNamara 2017) (register flag rv-eculizumab-c3-meningococcal).

Approval and licensure facts for checkpoint inhibitors, CAR T products and eculizumab are US (FDA) as reported in the cited sources; Philippine FDA registration and availability are not covered (register flag rv-immunotherapy-us-approvals).
